ExtraaLearn Project¶

Context¶

The EdTech industry has been surging in the past decade immensely, and according to a forecast, the Online Education market would be worth $286.62bn by 2023 with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.26% from 2018 to 2023. The modern era of online education has enforced a lot in its growth and expansion beyond any limit. Due to having many dominant features like ease of information sharing, personalized learning experience, transparency of assessment, etc, it is now preferable to traditional education.

In the present scenario due to the Covid-19, the online education sector has witnessed rapid growth and is attracting a lot of new customers. Due to this rapid growth, many new companies have emerged in this industry. With the availability and ease of use of digital marketing resources, companies can reach out to a wider audience with their offerings. The customers who show interest in these offerings are termed as leads. There are various sources of obtaining leads for Edtech companies, like

  • The customer interacts with the marketing front on social media or other online platforms.
  • The customer browses the website/app and downloads the brochure
  • The customer connects through emails for more information.

The company then nurtures these leads and tries to convert them to paid customers. For this, the representative from the organization connects with the lead on call or through email to share further details.

Objective¶

ExtraaLearn is an initial stage startup that offers programs on cutting-edge technologies to students and professionals to help them upskill/reskill. With a large number of leads being generated on a regular basis, one of the issues faced by ExtraaLearn is to identify which of the leads are more likely to convert so that they can allocate resources accordingly. You, as a data scientist at ExtraaLearn, have been provided the leads data to:

  • Analyze and build an ML model to help identify which leads are more likely to convert to paid customers,
  • Find the factors driving the lead conversion process
  • Create a profile of the leads which are likely to convert

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of leads and their interaction details with ExtraaLearn. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Data Dictionary

  • ID: ID of the lead

  • age: Age of the lead

  • current_occupation: Current occupation of the lead. Values include 'Professional','Unemployed',and 'Student'

  • first_interaction: How did the lead first interacted with ExtraaLearn. Values include 'Website', 'Mobile App'

  • profile_completed: What percentage of profile has been filled by the lead on the website/mobile app. Values include Low - (0-50%), Medium - (50-75%), High (75-100%)

  • website_visits: How many times has a lead visited the website

  • time_spent_on_website: Total time spent on the website

  • page_views_per_visit: Average number of pages on the website viewed during the visits.

  • last_activity: Last interaction between the lead and ExtraaLearn.

    • Email Activity: Seeking for details about program through email, Representative shared information with lead like brochure of program , etc
    • Phone Activity: Had a Phone Conversation with representative, Had conversation over SMS with representative, etc
    • Website Activity: Interacted on live chat with representative, Updated profile on website, etc

  • print_media_type1: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn in the Newspaper.

  • print_media_type2: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn in the Magazine.

  • digital_media: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn on the digital platforms.

  • educational_channels: Flag indicating whether the lead had heard about ExtraaLearn in the education channels like online forums, discussion threads, educational websites, etc.

  • referral: Flag indicating whether the lead had heard about ExtraaLearn through reference.

  • status: Flag indicating whether the lead was converted to a paid customer or not.

Questions

  1. Leads will have different expectations from the outcome of the course and the current occupation may play a key role in getting them to participate in the program. Find out how current occupation affects lead status.
  2. The company's first impression on the customer must have an impact. Do the first channels of interaction have an impact on the lead status?
  3. The company uses multiple modes to interact with prospects. Which way of interaction works best?
  4. The company gets leads from various channels such as print media, digital media, referrals, etc. Which of these channels have the highest lead conversion rate?
  5. People browsing the website or mobile application are generally required to create a profile by sharing their personal data before they can access additional information.Does having more details about a prospect increase the chances of conversion?

Observations:¶

*There is a left skew on the distribution of ages (median is higher than mean), with at least 75% of visitors being 57 years old, close to the maximum of 63.

  • There is a right skew on the distribution of website visits, with only 25% of visitors having visited more than five times, however the maximum number of visits is 30. Such elevated skewness suggests outliers.
  • There is a right skew on time spent on the_website, with again the likelihood of outliers.
  • There is a right skew as well on page views per visit. Again, with the same implication regarding outliers.
  • All numerical variables have elevated variance, which also warrants further analysis.
  • Approximately 30% of all leads have converted to paying customers based on the status.
  • Several variables have an unexpected minimum value of zero, including website_visits, time_spent_on_website and page_views_per_visit. This could affect the mean and the skew of the distributions.

Observations:

  • The skew in age distribution is remarkable, with approximately half of the non-converted leads ranging between 33 to 57 years of age, and half of the converted leads from 41 to 58.

  • Website visits are consistent between converted and non-converted leads, with a noted right skew as the majority of users seem to have visited the site less than 10 times.

  • Time spent on the website is not consistent between converted and non-converted leads, with half of the non-converted leads having left the website within 700 seconds, leading to a minimum, and then again a maximum for the remaining users around the 1800 seconds mark.

  • Page views per visit are distributed approximately normally among converted and non-converted groups.

  • For all metrics related to website visits, a number of users have not visited the website but have converted through other channels, including phone communication and email as previously discussed.

  • As expected, website_visits, time_spent_on_the_website and page_views_per_visit all present outliers.

# Select columns of type object (string) or category
categorical_vars = list(data.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns)

# Determine bounds
num_plots = len(categorical_vars)
total_cols = 2
total_rows = math.ceil(num_plots/total_cols)

# Size subplots dynamically
fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=total_rows, ncols=total_cols,
                        figsize=(7*total_cols, 7*total_rows), constrained_layout=False)

# Render countplots, with hue
for i, var in enumerate(categorical_vars):
    row = i//total_cols
    pos = i % total_cols

    if (i < len(categorical_vars)): plot = sns.countplot(x=var, data=data, ax=axs[row][pos], hue='status')

# Delete extraneous subplot
fig.delaxes(axs[total_rows-1][total_cols-1])

Observations: bold textBased on the visualization, we can answer some of the questions asked initially

  1. Leads will have different expectations from the outcome of the course and the current occupation may play a key role in getting them to participate in the program. Find out how
    current occupation affects lead status. Based on the above observations, it seems that couse is getting more leads by the unemployed and professionals than those by Students. Also among those , working professionals converted more inot the paying customers. Apparently, they are joinin the course to upskill or reskill.

  2. The company's first impression on the customer must have an impact. Do the first channels of interaction have an impact on the lead status? There seems to be significantly higher rate of conversion for those who had website interactions.

  3. The company uses multiple modes to interact with prospects. Which way of interaction works best?
    The mode of interaction that works the best is E mail activity as it shows the higher rate of success than other modes. Email Activity 49.392888 Phone Activity 26.756288 Website Activity 23.850824.

  4. The company gets leads from various channels such as print media, digital media, referrals, etc. Which of these channels have the highest lead conversion rate?
    It is difficult to identify conversion rates according to channel through visualization alone. We will further analyze this by computing the individual conversion rates for each channel. Even though theere re no but customers have converte to paid customers. so further analysis will only clarify it.

  5. People browsing the website or mobile application are generally required to create a profile by sharing their personal data before they can access additional information.Does having more details about a prospect increase the chances of ]conversion?
    It seems obvious that persons who have completed the additional information have more conversions

To better estimate conversion rates in relation to advertising channels, we can calculate the raw conversion rate for each channel.

This will not provide conclusive indications however, in part because conversion rates could depend on users having been reached through multiple channels. For this, we should consider feature engineering, and further study.

However it will help to highlight the impact of each individual channel among converted users.

The violin plots suggest that age distribution is relatively consistent across the different categories of these categorical variables, and the bimodal age distribution (peaks in late 30s and late 50s) is a general characteristic of the leads in this dataset.

Status and Time Spent on Website Earlier we've noted a possible correlation between status (converted leads), and time spent on website. So we will explore this relationship.

In [32]:
sns.violinplot(data = data, y = 'time_spent_on_website', hue = 'status')
plt.show()

Observations:

The violin plot confirms a skew toward longer time spent on website among converted leads, with a minimum around 1000 seconds. By contrast, most non-converted leads are active for less than 700 seconds. This could indicate that both categories of leads have spent an initial research and onboarding phase, and once signed up, that converted leads have continued to use the website for longer periods of time. In a general sense, it suggests positive correlation between conversion and time spent on the website. However, exactly how that time is spent calls for further study.

Observation Both the groups show a similar overall pattern of being skewed to the right, it appears that converted leads (orange) tend to have a slightly higher frequency of more page views per visit compared to non-converted leads (blue). The peak for converted leads seems to be shifted slightly to the right, and there are more converted leads in the bins representing higher page views per visit.

This suggests that leads who view more pages per visit are somewhat more likely to convert, which aligns with our earlier observation from the univariate analysis of this variable.

# Creating metric function

def metrics_score(actual, predicted):

    print(classification_report(actual, predicted))

    cm = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted)

    plt.figure(figsize = (8, 5))

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot = True, fmt = '.2f', xticklabels = ['Not Converting', 'Converting'], yticklabels = ['Not Converting', 'Converting'])
    plt.ylabel('Actual')

    plt.xlabel('Predicted')

    plt.show()
In [50]:
 def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier

    predictors: independent variables

    target: dependent variable
    """

    # Predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    recall = recall_score(target, pred,average = 'macro')                 # To compute recall

    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average = 'macro')              # To compute precision

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)                                 # To compute accuracy score


    # Creating a dataframe of metrics

    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Precision":  precision,
            "Recall":  recall,
            "Accuracy": acc,
        },

        index = [0],
    )

    return df_perf

All the performace values, i.e. precision, Recall, and F1-score, are all one which means the model has achieved the perfect precision and accuracy. 2585 (True Negative) will not attriate and 1103(True Positive) will attriate there is no or zero **false negative. ** The model has achieved perfect performance training data. Althought this is an ideal performance, but this might be a case of overfitting. Overfitting means training data fits too well, even including the noise and specific patters of the training set which can be misleading for the the test data.

Out[81]:
Precision Recall Accuracy
0 0.783153 0.768577 0.816901

Observation: Precision, Recall, and F1-score:
Class 0 (Not Converting):
Precision: 0.86 (86% of leads predicted as not converting actually didn't convert)
Recall: 0.89 (89% of leads that didn't convert were correctly identified)
F1-score: 0.87 (Harmonic mean of precision and recall for class 0)
Class 1 (Converting):
Precision: 0.71 (71% of leads predicted as converting actually converted)
Recall: 0.65 (65% of leads that converted were correctly identified)
F1-score: 0.68 (Harmonic mean of precision and recall for class 1)
Compared to the perfect performance on the training data, the performance on the test data is significantly lower. This confirms the overfitting we suspected. The model learned the training data too specifically and is not generalizing as well to new, unseen data.

Specifically, the model is better at predicting leads that will not convert (Class 0) than leads that will convert (Class 1). The lower recall for Class 1 (0.65) means that the model missed about 35% of the leads that actually converted (resulting in 96 False Negatives). This is important because identifying leads who are likely to convert is crucial for the company's objective.

HyperParameter Tuning The criterion is to measure the quality of a split. Supported criteria are “gini” for the Gini impurity and “entropy” for the information gain. The GridSearch function is used for hyperparameter tuning

After hyperparameter tuning, the model's performance on the training data shows a trade-off. It has become very effective at identifying nearly all of the converting leads (high recall for Class 1), but it also incorrectly flags a large number of non-converting leads as potential converters (high number of False Positives for Class 0 and low recall for Class 0).

This contrasts with the initial untuned model, which had perfect scores on the training data due to overfitting. The tuned model is no longer perfectly fitting the training data but is instead showing a performance profile that is likely influenced by the hyperparameter tuning process, particularly if class weights were used to prioritize identifying the minority class (converting leads).

Precision Recall Accuracy
0 0.697977 0.677966 0.547129

Precision: The tuned Decision Tree has a lower precision (0.698) compared to the untuned Decision Tree (0.783).
Recall: The tuned Decision Tree also has a lower recall (0.678) compared to the untuned Decision Tree (0.769). Correction: In a previous turn, the recall for the tuned Decision Tree on the test set from the metrics_score output was 1.00 for Class 1. The model_performance_classification function calculates macro average recall, which is why the value here is lower. The macro average recall considers the recall of both classes equally.
Accuracy: The tuned Decision Tree has significantly lower accuracy (0.547) compared to the untuned Decision Tree (0.817).

Based on the macro average metrics provided by model_performance_classification, the untuned Decision Tree appears to perform better on the test data in terms of overall precision, recall, and accuracy.

It's important to note the difference between the macro average recall shown here and the recall for a specific class (like Class 1) shown in the classification_report output from the metrics_score function. The model_performance_classification function provides a summary across both classes, while the metrics_score function provides detailed metrics for each class individually.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

With Random Forest we have created a model with elevated recall and overall good performance to predict leads likely to convert (~89% recall).

Based on feature importance from classification as well as EDA, factors contributing to conversion seem to be:

Time spent on the website Having one's first interaction through the website Profile completeness at or above medium Followed by: Professional activity **(non-student) **Age (toward late career) Last activity was through the website Also: Referrals could be playing a role into the conversion decision. Based on these, leads most likely to convert are late-career professionals, employed or unemployed, who have engaged with and spent significant time on the website, and possibly completed their profile.

EDA however has indicated some problems:

The impact of advertising channels is not represented well in the model, with insufficient sample sizes. The data also doesn't describe possible correlations and the combined effects of multiple advertising channels. Conversion rates among leads who have joined without visiting the website are lower than the average. Conversion rates among leads who have interacted first with the mobile application are significantly lower. The data doesn't provide indications about how time is spent on the website.

Conclusion from the Comparison:

Based on these macro-averaged metrics, the Tuned Random Forest classifier appears to be the best overall performing model on the test data. It achieves the highest accuracy and macro-averaged recall, and a very competitive macro-averaged precision. The Gradientboost classifier is also a strong contender with very similar performance. This comparison table is useful in deciding which model to deploy keeping in mind the precific business goals and which metrics are most important such as maximizing recall for converting leads vs minimizing false positives vers overall accuracy.
